query: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has high strength at room temperature and elevated temperature but a relatively high density of 10.21 g cm−3. What single intervention could reduce its density without sacrificing its mechanical properties at room temperature and at elevated temperatures, including approximately 1000 °C? State the proposed intervention and mechanism, predict directional changes relative to as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, define the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, identify supporting prior evidence, and propose an experiment and rejection criterion that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Replacing the high‐density Ta in as‐cast HfMoTaTiZr with Nb (i.e. converting it to an HfMoNbTiZr alloy) will lower the overall density without sacrificing its high strength and ductility at room temperature and near 1000 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: As‐cast HfMoTaTiZr refractory high‐entropy alloy with a density of approximately 10.21 g/cm³.
generation.intervention: Replace Ta with Nb in the alloy formulation, so that Ta is substituted by Nb while keeping the other elements unchanged.
generation.conditions: Standard as‐cast processing with mechanical testing performed at room temperature and at elevated temperatures up to approximately 1000 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: The substitution leads to modified atomic-scale solid-solution effects and lattice distortions. Nb, having a lower atomic mass than Ta, decreases the average density while still contributing to a BCC-type solid solution that supports high strength and ductility.
generation.mechanism: Nb’s lower density compared to Ta will reduce the overall mass of the alloy; concurrently, Nb is known to promote ductility and has a relatively mild effect on yield strength loss at elevated temperatures. This substitution maintains solid solution strengthening and a stable high-temperature microstructure, thereby preserving mechanical performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Nb-substituted alloy (HfMoNbTiZr) is expected to exhibit a significantly reduced density relative to 10.21 g/cm³ while achieving yield strengths and ductilities at room temperature and at ~1000 °C that are comparable to or improved over the original HfMoTaTiZr alloy.
generation.baseline: Current mechanical properties and density of as-cast HfMoTaTiZr with high strength but relatively high density (10.21 g/cm³).
generation.boundary: Measurements are limited to as-cast alloys under conditions without additional thermo-mechanical processing, with mechanical testing performed at room temperature and elevated temperatures up to about 1000 °C.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative reductions in density and the full impact on phase stability and high-temperature performance require experimental validation; there is uncertainty regarding the exact trade-offs in mechanical performance after substitution.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of alloys under the same as-cast conditions: one with the original HfMoTaTiZr composition and one with Ta replaced by Nb (HfMoNbTiZr). Measure the density of each alloy (e.g., via Archimedes' method). Conduct standardized mechanical tests (e.g., compressive or tensile tests) at room temperature and at an elevated temperature around 1000 °C.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Nb-substituted alloy does not show a significant reduction in density compared to the original HfMoTaTiZr, or if it exhibits a meaningful degradation in strength or ductility at room temperature or near 1000 °C, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

The equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy was chosen to analyze the effect of each constituent elemental by the subtraction method and, thus, HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi were studied. Among these alloys, HfMoNbTaTi has the best mechanical performance, that is, 27% compressive strain at room temperature and yield strength 367 MPa at 1400 °C. HfMoNbTaTi has great potential for elevated-temperature applications. As the alloy system does not contain very expensive elements such as Re and Ru, it is cost competitive for high-temperature applications like Nb-Hf-Ti alloys in space vehicles. Further modification of composition and/or anti-oxidation coatings are still required for high-temperature applications in the air. According to the experiment results, the effects of Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr on mechanical properties of equiatomic Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr alloys were described. For higher room-temperature strength, one should add an element which interacts frequently with the alloy, such as Mo.
